title: DESIGN ENGINEERING: BUILD A MOTION STUDIO AROUND OPUS 5.5
html:
Anyone can prompt an animation. Few know how to direct one.
Opus 5.5 does the typing. You still bring the taste.
At the end of this article, you’ll learn how to…
Explain what design engineering is and why it matters
Assemble a motion studio from free and low-cost tools
Set up Claude Opus 5.5 as your planning and building partner
Turn a rough idea into a timed motion brief
Build animations three ways: Claude’s builders, Figma Motion, and Lottie files
Write prompts with a role, context, task, constraints, and output format
Export your work as video, GIF, web page, or Lottie file
Follow a seven-day plan to make the skill stick


Design engineering in plain English

Design engineering means making a design actually work, not just look right. A designer decides how something should look and feel. A developer writes code, the written instructions a computer follows. A design engineer does both, and AI now handles much of the typing.
That matters most for motion. Motion is movement in a design: a button that reacts when pressed, a chart that draws itself, a logo that assembles. It shows people where to look and what just changed. It also makes a prototype, a rough working version you can test before building the real thing, feel real.
This guide builds that skill with one AI model and a few tools. No coding background needed.
Words you’ll see
HTML and CSS: the two languages web pages are written in. HTML holds the content; CSS controls looks and movement.
Artifact: Claude’s name for something it builds for you, like a page, design, or animation, that opens beside the chat.
Keyframe: a marked moment on a timeline where you set how something looks. Software fills in the motion between keyframes.
Easing: how motion speeds up and slows down so it feels natural, not robotic.
MP4, WebM, GIF, SVG: two video formats, a looping image, and a scalable drawing file. FPS means frames per second; higher is smoother.
Lottie: a small file format that stores animation as data, so apps and sites can play it sharply.
Beta: a feature still being tested, so it may change.
Context window: how much text a model can keep in view at once.
Frame and Smart Animate: in Figma, a frame is a screen-sized canvas. Smart Animate animates between two frames by matching layers that share a name.

What a “motion studio” means here

A motion studio here is a repeatable workflow, not a room full of gear. One AI model plans and builds. A few tools animate, preview, and export. You loop through five steps: brief, build, look, fix, export.

Which path are you on?
Free plan: Claude Design and Figma, but not Opus.
Pro or Max: add Opus 5.5 and Claude Code.
Team or Enterprise: add Claude Motion. Every project below works without Motion unless noted.

Why build around Opus 5.5

Opus 5.5 is Anthropic’s newest Opus model, released September 22, 2026. Everything below comes from Anthropic’s own pages.
Cheaper and faster. Anthropic says it costs about 40% less than Opus 5 on typical workloads and writes output over 30% faster. Developers pay $4 per million input tokens (small chunks of text) and $20 per million output tokens; subscribers pay their plan price within usage limits.
Clearer writing. It puts key information first, uses less jargon, and follows writing rules you give it. That suits briefs and handoff notes.
Better at reading visuals. Anthropic’s guide says it reads charts, diagrams, and screenshots more accurately than Opus 5, including what changed between two versions of a diagram. Screenshots make useful feedback.
Visual polish. In one outside test where several Claude models each built a game from a single prompt, Opus 5.5 scored highest for graphics and polish. That’s one test, not a promise.
Long jobs. It has a 1 million-token context window and up to 128,000 tokens of output per reply.
Easy to reach. It’s in the Claude app on Pro and above, and it’s the default model in Claude Code on Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise accounts.
Honest limits
With no design direction, it falls back on a few default styles, per Anthropic. “Avoid a generic AI look” mostly swaps one default for another, so name the styles to avoid.
Anthropic says Claude Motion builds animation by writing code and uses no video-generation model. Treat the whole stack that way: Claude writes instructions, and the tools do the moving.
Thinking can’t be turned off. The default effort setting (how long it thinks) is medium in Claude Code and the API. Raise it only after you see a quality gain.
Anthropic says benchmark margins are a weak guide to real-world differences. Test on your own work, starting with Project 1.

Step-by-step setup
Pick a plan. Opus isn’t on the Free plan, so choose Pro or above. Open claude.ai and look for Opus in the model picker.
Expected result: Opus 5.5 is selectable. If not, check your plan.
Turn on file creation. Go to Settings > Capabilities and switch on “Create and edit files.” Artifacts need it.
Expected result: a requested page or design opens beside the chat.
Write your studio rules. One page covering brand colors, fonts, tone, and motion limits like “nothing slower than 600 ms.” Save it in a Project, a workspace that keeps related chats and documents together, and paste it at the start of chats.
Expected result: every session starts with the same rules.
Run a design test. In a chat, choose Output > Design and ask for “a one-screen welcome page for [PRODUCT].” On Team or Enterprise, also try Output > Motion with “Animate [IDEA] in 15 seconds.” (Enterprise owners must switch Motion on first, under Organization settings > Artifacts.)
Expected result: an editable canvas opens, and Export lists HTML, PDF, and PowerPoint. Motion exports MP4.
Open Figma Motion. Make a free Figma account, open a design file, and click Motion in the toolbar. You need edit access to the file.
Expected result: a timeline appears along the bottom of the screen.
Optional: add Claude Code. Download the Claude desktop app, sign in on a paid plan, and open the Code tab. Ask: “make me a simple webpage that says hello world.” Approve the file creation, then double-click the HTML file. Prefer a terminal (a text window where you type commands)? The terminal guide walks you through it. Opus 5.5 needs Claude Code v2.1.280 or later; claude update upgrades it.
Expected result: a page opens in your browser.
Optional: add Lottie and Rive. Create free accounts at LottieFiles and Rive.
Expected result: you can preview a Lottie file and open Rive’s editor.

Mini projects
Six projects, beginner to advanced. Every prompt has a role, context, task, constraints, and output format. Replace everything in [BRACKETS].
Project 1 (beginner): Motion brief from a vague idea

Goal: Turn an idea into a timed storyboard you can build from.
Tools: Claude with Opus 5.5, chat only.

Good output: Scene times add up to your total. Each scene says what moves. The questions are specific, like “Should the logo end centered or bottom-left?”
Project 2 (beginner): Animated logo reveal

Goal: A 3-second logo animation as one web page.
Tools: Claude Design (Output > Design).

Good output: It plays smoothly on load and doesn’t jump at the end. Changing one timing number changes the speed. Export > standalone HTML gives you a file that opens in a browser.
Project 3 (beginner): Button and loader motion in Figma

Goal: Add a pressed state and a looping loader.
Tools: Figma Motion, plus Claude for the spec.

Good output: The press feels instant, not floaty. The loader loops without a visible jump. If you use Smart Animate, layer names match across frames.
Project 4 (intermediate): 30-second data explainer

Goal: Animate one chart’s story for a meeting.
Tools: Claude Motion (Team or Enterprise). On other plans, ask Claude Design for an animated page instead.

Good output: Every number matches your source. Each scene carries one idea. Export a short test first: Anthropic’s help article lists no maximum length or resolution.
Project 5 (intermediate): Animated landing-page hero

Goal: A hero section with entrance motion and a button hover, exported as HTML.
Tools: Claude Design, then Export > standalone HTML.

Good output: It looks like your references, not a template. None of the avoided styles appear. The motion values are listed so you can adjust them.
Project 6 (advanced): Figma to Lottie, then check it

Goal: Ship a 3-second loop as a Lottie file and verify it.
Tools: Figma Motion, LottieFiles, Claude.
Steps: Build the loop in Figma Motion. In Export, open the Animated tab and pick Lottie or dotLottie. Test it in the Lottie player you’ll ship with. Screenshot both versions.

Good output: Specific findings, like “the angular gradient became a flat image; swap in a linear one.” If the images match, it says so.

Prompt library
Ten prompts. Paste your studio rules first, then swap every [BRACKET].
1. Studio rules writer

2. Reference teardown

3. Storyboard to keyframes

4. Easing and timing picker

5. Direction without the default look

6. HTML and CSS animation builder

7. Feedback translator

8. Accessibility and performance check

9. Developer handoff note

10. Claude Code motion guide


Common mistakes and fixes


Your 7-day practice plan
Spend about 45 minutes a day.
Day 1, set up. Finish steps 1–5 and write your studio rules.
Day 2, brief. Run Project 1 on a real idea, twice. Compare the results.
Day 3, first motion. Do Project 2. Change three timing numbers and watch what happens.
Day 4, Figma. Do Project 3. Try presets first, then keyframes, then Figma’s agent.
Day 5, explain with motion. Do Project 4, using Motion if your plan has it.
Day 6, make it yours. Do Project 5 after running library prompt 5 for three directions.
Day 7, ship. Do Project 6, write a handoff with prompt 9, and save your best prompts beside your studio rules.
You don't need animation software or a coding background to ship motion. You need a good brief.
